profile.address: Turner McDonald Parkway, Alpharetta, Fulton County, Georgia, 30009
profile.reading:
This building sits on Turner McDonald Parkway, a frontage road that parallels Georgia state route 400 through the Alpharetta and North Fulton technology corridor -- an area that has hosted large enterprise computing operations for Hewlett-Packard and its corporate predecessors for decades. The corridor's HP presence traces back to Electronic Data Systems (EDS), the Texas-founded IT-outsourcing company that built a major campus presence in metro Atlanta serving large corporate and government clients. Hewlett-Packard acquired EDS in 2008 and folded its operations into HP's own enterprise-services division, later renamed Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) when HP split into two public companies in 2015.

In the early 2010s, HP undertook a well-documented, worldwide "mega-datacenter consolidation," collapsing roughly 85 smaller data centers into six large regional hubs across three U.S. metro areas as part of a stated $600 million infrastructure investment intended to cut internal IT spending by roughly $1 billion. The plan called for two new 200,000-square-foot data centers in the Atlanta area -- one in Suwanee and one in Alpharetta, the latter built "at an existing HP campus location" -- each projected to employ about 140 people, using a modular, remotely managed "lights-out" design intended to cut cooling costs by up to a quarter. Separately, in 2017 HPE spun off its Enterprise Services division into DXC Technology, and some former HP/EDS data-center real estate in the Alpharetta area -- including a building at a different address on Westside Parkway -- transferred into DXC's ownership under the name "Enterprise Services LLC," which DXC's own facility records describe as "formerly known as Hewlett Packard Enterprise Data Center."

Public sources do not identify this specific Turner McDonald Parkway building by street number, confirm its square footage or power capacity, or state definitively whether it is the Alpharetta consolidation project described above, a legacy EDS-era building, or a separate HPE facility retained after the DXC spinoff. Neither HPE's corporate site nor Fulton County's public property records return an address-level match for this exact location through ordinary search, and the road itself runs through parts of Alpharetta, Roswell, and Sandy Springs, which complicates pinning the building down further from public mapping alone.

What can be said with confidence is that this is an internal corporate data center supporting Hewlett Packard Enterprise's own IT operations, not a colocation facility marketed to outside tenants. That distinction matters for why so little is published about it: HPE, like most large technology companies, discloses detailed specifications for space it leases commercially to customers, but treats its own internal infrastructure -- including buildings like this one -- as a private operational asset with no public disclosure obligation, leaving local incentive records, permits, or company statements as the only realistic paths to more detail.
